newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba heading out of recession, minister says.
newsitem.headline: Cuba heading out of recession, minister says.

text.p: Cuba is still working under an emergency economic programme but the worst of the recent recession is over and the economy should grow over the next few years, Economy Minister Jose Luis Rodriguez said.

Rodriguez, in an interview released on Saturday by the Cuban news agency Prensa Latina, said the pace of future growth would depend on the level of external financing the island could obtain. Excessive dependence on costly, short-term financing was currently the biggest problem facing the economy.

"We're still in the situation of an emergency economic programme, what we call the Special Period. It would be risky to predict how much longer it could last, but there are factors which allow us to state that the most critical period is behind us," Rodriguez, who is also a government Vice-President, said.
"The growth rates over the next few years won't be low. I mean, we won't have a contraction again," he added.

The Cuban government reported Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth of 7.8 percent in 1996. This followed GDP growth of 2.5 percent in 1995, 0.7 percent in 1994 and a sharp negative contraction in GDP of nearly 35 percent between 1989 and 1993.
This last period marked the severe economic recession triggered by the collapse of communist-ruled Cuba's trade with the former Soviet bloc, its main supplier for 30 years.

Rodriguez said the government forecast continued growth this year, but at a slower rate than in 1996, because it wanted to resolve the problem of external financing, in which Cuba was forced to depend on short-term credits for its long-term development investment. The island was being forced to rely on one-year credits at average interest of around 14 percent.
An official government forecast forsees GDP growth of between four and five percent in 1997.

Rodriguez said Cuba's accumulated short-term debt, combined with the reviving economy's growing need for working and investment capital, was squeezing the balance of payments. This squeeze was worsened by the effects of the U.S. Helms-Burton law, which had delayed credits and made them more expensive.
The Helms-Burton law, introduced a year ago, threatens penalties against foreign investors who do business on property expropriated from U.S. interests following Castro's 1959 revolution.
Rodriguez said this law had failed in its aim to halt foreign investment in Cuba and, under these circumstances, the country's economic performance was "reasonably good".
The minister said priority would continue to be given to hard-currency earning sectors like tourism, the sugar and nickel industries, fisheries and tobacco production.
